title: Kharda Marks the Confederacy's High Tide

title_i18n.en: Kharda Marks the Confederacy's High Tide

subtitle: Kharda, 1795 – The Last Crest of the Maratha Tide
figure: Parshuram Bhau Patwardhan and Nizam Ali Khan
era: Late Maratha confederacy and Hyderabad, 1795 CE
moral: A confederacy can win its greatest field and still reveal how fragile unity has become.

sources.citation: Peshwa Daftar Marathi state papers and correspondence for the Kharda campaign, ed. G.S. Sardesai and others
sources.note: Contemporary Maratha administrative papers from the Peshwa's side, strongest for negotiations, claims and command politics.

sources.citation: Kharda Yuddhachi Bakhar, Marathi campaign chronicle, late 18th/early 19th century tradition
sources.note: Maratha narrative tradition; useful for names and memory but to be checked against state papers.

sources.citation: Governor-General John Shore's correspondence and East India Company records, 1795
sources.note: Contemporary British observer record explaining non-intervention despite the Nizam's expectations.

sources.citation: G.S. Sardesai, New History of the Marathas, Vol. III (1948); Jadunath Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire, Vol. IV (1950); James Grant Duff, A History of the Mahrattas, Vol. III (1826)
sources.note: Modern and early colonial syntheses comparing Maratha, Hyderabad and British evidence.

panels.shot: split-panel wide, half showing a Maratha host on dusty Deccan plain, half showing the Nizam’s camp clustered around Kharda fort

dialogue.text: In 1795, at Kharda, Parshuram Bhau Patwardhan and Nizam Ali Khan fought a war born of arrears and insult—and the Maratha confederacy won its greatest field even as its foundations quietly cracked.

panels.shot: wide establishing shot of the Deccan plateau at dusk

dialogue.text: By the late eighteenth century, the Mughal centre had faded, and the Deccan was ruled by powers that once served it—Marathas in Poona, the Nizam in Hyderabad, each measuring rank and tribute more sharply than ever.

panels.shot: intercut medium close-ups, left Parshuram Bhau in Poona durbar, right Nizam Ali Khan in Hyderabad court

dialogue.text: Maratha papers speak of arrears due from Hyderabad and of a minister’s slight to the Peshwa; in Hyderabad, Nizam Ali Khan chafed at Maratha suzerainty and the tone of their envoys.

panels.shot: over-the-shoulder close-up from behind Parshuram Bhau, looking at a crumpled letter from Hyderabad

dialogue.text: The Peshwa’s correspondence, preserved in the Daftar, shows tempers rising note by note—claims of unpaid sums, disputes over territory, and the demand that the Nizam dismiss the minister blamed for insult.

panels.shot: medium shot of Nizam Ali Khan in council with British and French officers

dialogue.text: To strengthen his hand, the Nizam turned to European expertise—Frenchmen like Michel Raymond drilled his infantry, while British residents weighed promises and policy from Calcutta.

panels.shot: wide battlefield council shot under a tent in the Maratha camp

dialogue.text: For this quarrel, the Maratha houses gathered: troops from the Peshwa, Scindia, Holkar, Bhonsle, Gaekwad—each with its own pride and grievances—but for once riding under a common cause.

panels.shot: low-angle wide shot of the Maratha army on the march

dialogue.text: The Daftar names Parshuram Bhau as commander in the field; under his eye, the confederacy moved toward the Nizam’s forces near the small fort of Kharda, each ally counting both honour and share.

panels.shot: wide shot of opposing camps with Kharda fort between

dialogue.text: On 11 March 1795, near Kharda, the two hosts at last faced each other—Maratha cavalry massed in loose depth, and the Nizam’s mixed army, including Raymond’s French-drilled battalions, drawn up nearer the fort.

panels.shot: dynamic mid-wide of the battle’s opening movements

dialogue.text: Contemporary accounts differ on numbers and on which contingent struck hardest, but they agree: Raymond’s corps pressed forward in European order, while Maratha horse and guns hunted for the open edges.

panels.shot: close, slightly low-angle shot on Parshuram Bhau amid battle

dialogue.text: Bakhar tradition glorifies sudden charges and single heroes; modern historians, comparing papers and letters, emphasise instead the steady pressure of Maratha manoeuvre and the commanders’ use of the terrain.

panels.shot: medium shot of Nizam Ali Khan watching his lines bend back toward Kharda

dialogue.text: The Nizam’s army did not break at once; it fell back toward Kharda. But as it withdrew into the fort’s shadow, the Marathas moved quickly to cut the roads and water, turning field battle into siege.

panels.shot: wide shot of Kharda fort ringed by Maratha positions

dialogue.text: Kharda was no great metropolis, but its walls now held the Nizam’s main force. The Marathas settled in, their siege lines drawing a hard ring around allies and adversaries alike inside.

panels.shot: closer shot of Maratha siege camp life at night

dialogue.text: The siege tightened day by day. Letters from the camp track disputes over shares of plunder and command, yet also show the houses holding together long enough to keep the Nizam’s army penned.

panels.shot: interior shot inside Kharda fort, dim and tense

dialogue.text: Inside Kharda, supplies ran low. Later historians, using both Maratha and Hyderabad sources, describe mounting shortages and pressure, the Nizam’s commanders urging either a desperate breakout or terms.

panels.shot: medium shot of a British envoy in Hyderabad receiving news

dialogue.text: The Nizam had hoped for British arms against the Marathas, but Governor-General John Shore’s letters from Calcutta tell another story: the Company would not yet fight the confederacy on Hyderabad’s behalf.

panels.shot: medium shot of Nizam Ali Khan receiving envoys from the Maratha camp

dialogue.text: Cut off and without British support, the Nizam opened serious negotiations. The settlement that followed, recorded in Maratha and British sources, demanded money, land, and the surrender of the minister blamed for insult.

panels.shot: close shot of a treaty document being sealed

dialogue.text: The terms forced territorial concessions and indemnity. The minister whose words had sparked outrage was given up. For the Maratha houses, this was vindication; for the Nizam, it was a chastening loss.

panels.shot: wide shot of Maratha leaders in camp after the victory, dawn light

dialogue.text: Kharda was the last great unified victory of the Maratha confederacy over another major Indian power. Yet even in the afterglow, papers record quarrels over credit, reward and future policy.

panels.shot: time-lapse style composite: Kharda battlefield fading into later scenes of British troops in the Deccan

dialogue.text: Within a decade, Assaye and the Second Anglo-Maratha War would show a different tide—Kharda stands not as a rescue of empire, but as its high-water mark, a reminder of how unity can peak even as decline begins.
